sentence: Which revision correctly distributes the two clauses?
setupText: A draft reads, 'Only after did the researchers release the raw data the criticism become persuasive.' Repair it without changing which event preceded the other.
taskText: Which revision correctly distributes the two clauses?
text: A draft reads, 'Only after did the researchers release the raw data the criticism become persuasive.' Repair it without changing which event preceded the other. Which revision correctly distributes the two clauses?
options: Only after the criticism became persuasive did the researchers release the raw data.
Only after did the researchers release the raw data did the criticism become persuasive.
Only after the researchers did release the raw data the criticism became persuasive.
Only after the researchers released the raw data did the criticism become persuasive.
answer: Only after the researchers released the raw data did the criticism become persuasive.
explanation: The release remains in the ordinary-order after-clause; 'did' belongs in the main clause about the criticism.

rationales.Only after the researchers released the: The release remains in the ordinary-order after-clause; 'did' belongs in the main clause about the criticism.
rationales.Only after the criticism became persuasi: This is grammatical but reverses the event sequence.
rationales.Only after did the researchers release t: The main clause is repaired, but the subordinate after-clause still has inappropriate inversion.
rationales.Only after the researchers did release t: Emphatic 'did release' can be grammatical inside the after-clause, but it does not supply the required main-clause inversion.

sentence: Why does only sentence 2 use auxiliary inversion?
setupText: Compare (1) 'Not only the proposal but also the pilot study reduced costs' and (2) 'Not only did the proposal reduce costs; it also simplified reporting.'
taskText: Why does only sentence 2 use auxiliary inversion?
text: Compare (1) 'Not only the proposal but also the pilot study reduced costs' and (2) 'Not only did the proposal reduce costs; it also simplified reporting.' Why does only sentence 2 use auxiliary inversion?
options: Sentence 1 lacks an auxiliary because two subjects cannot share one.
In 1, not only is inside the subject; in 2, it introduces a negative-focused clause.
Sentence 2 uses inversion because reporting happens later than cost reduction.
Sentence 1 is incorrect because every initial 'not only' requires inversion.
answer: In 1, not only is inside the subject; in 2, it introduces a negative-focused clause.
explanation: A not-only subject phrase keeps ordinary order, while fronted clausal not only triggers auxiliary inversion.

rationales.Sentence 1 lacks an auxiliary because tw: A coordinated subject can share an auxiliary; subject structure, not a ban on shared auxiliaries, explains this order.
rationales.In 1, not only is inside the subject; in: A not-only subject phrase keeps ordinary order, while fronted clausal not only triggers auxiliary inversion.
rationales.Sentence 2 uses inversion because report: The structure does not establish that chronology; inversion follows the fronted expression.
rationales.Sentence 1 is incorrect because every in: Initial position alone is insufficient: 'not only' can be part of the subject, as in 1.

sentence: Which rewrite meets all three requirements?
setupText: Rewrite 'Such a short memo had seldom been discussed at such length' with 'Seldom' first. Preserve the past perfect passive.
taskText: Which rewrite meets all three requirements?
text: Rewrite 'Such a short memo had seldom been discussed at such length' with 'Seldom' first. Preserve the past perfect passive. Which rewrite meets all three requirements?
options: Seldom had such a short memo been discussed at such length.
Seldom had been such a short memo discussed at such length.
Seldom was such a short memo discussed at such length.
Seldom had such a short memo discussed at such length.
answer: Seldom had such a short memo been discussed at such length.
focusKey: coverage-inversion-and-emphasis-c1-1763:Inverting only the finite member of an auxiliary chain
explanation: The first auxiliary crosses the subject while the rest of the passive perfect stays together after it.

rationales.Seldom had been such a short memo discus: Only the finite auxiliary 'had' precedes the subject; 'been discussed' follows it.
rationales.Seldom was such a short memo discussed a: This is grammatical but changes the past perfect to the simple past passive.
rationales.Seldom had such a short memo been discus: The first auxiliary crosses the subject while the rest of the passive perfect stays together after it.
rationales.Seldom had such a short memo discussed a: Omitting 'been' removes the passive, leaving the memo as an implausibly incomplete active subject.

sentence: Which pseudo-cleft precisely identifies what remains unclear?
setupText: The policy lists permissible exceptions but does not identify the person authorized to approve them. Highlight that omission.
taskText: Which pseudo-cleft precisely identifies what remains unclear?
text: The policy lists permissible exceptions but does not identify the person authorized to approve them. Highlight that omission. Which pseudo-cleft precisely identifies what remains unclear?
options: What the policy leaves unclear is whether any exceptions are permitted.
What the policy leaves unclear is why no exceptions may be approved.
What the policy leaves unclear is who may approve the listed exceptions.
Who may approve the listed exceptions is clearly stated in the policy.
answer: What the policy leaves unclear is who may approve the listed exceptions.
explanation: The what-cleft frames an information gap, and the embedded who-clause specifies that the missing information is the decision-maker.

rationales.What the policy leaves unclear is whethe: Permission for the listed exceptions is established; the unidentified authority is the gap.
rationales.What the policy leaves unclear is why no: This invents a blanket refusal of exceptions, contrary to the context.
rationales.Who may approve the listed exceptions is: This reverses the absence of the approval authority.
rationales.What the policy leaves unclear is who ma: The what-cleft frames an information gap, and the embedded who-clause specifies that the missing information is the decision-maker.

sentence: What is B primarily doing with the cleft?
setupText: A: 'You reject the model's calculations, then?' B: 'It is the assumption behind the model that I find problematic.'
taskText: What is B primarily doing with the cleft?
text: A: 'You reject the model's calculations, then?' B: 'It is the assumption behind the model that I find problematic.' What is B primarily doing with the cleft?
options: Confirming that both the assumption and all the calculations are wrong.
Withdrawing criticism of the model as a whole.
Redirecting the criticism from the calculations to their underlying assumption.
Asking A to identify which assumption the model uses.
answer: Redirecting the criticism from the calculations to their underlying assumption.
explanation: The noun phrase in cleft focus replaces A's proposed target; it does not by itself establish that every calculation is sound.

rationales.Redirecting the criticism from the calcu: The noun phrase in cleft focus replaces A's proposed target; it does not by itself establish that every calculation is sound.
rationales.Confirming that both the assumption and: The reply identifies an assumption as the target; it does not endorse that broader verdict.
rationales.Withdrawing criticism of the model as a: B still identifies something problematic within the model.
rationales.Asking A to identify which assumption th: The declarative cleft states B's criticism rather than requesting information.

sentence: Which version preserves the prohibition and places inversion correctly?
setupText: The director said that interview notes must never leave the research team. Report the instruction with 'under no circumstances' at the start of the embedded that-clause.
taskText: Which version preserves the prohibition and places inversion correctly?
text: The director said that interview notes must never leave the research team. Report the instruction with 'under no circumstances' at the start of the embedded that-clause. Which version preserves the prohibition and places inversion correctly?
options: The director said that under no circumstances interview notes should leave the research team.
Under no circumstances did the director say that interview notes should leave the research team.
The director said that under no circumstances should interview notes remain within the research team.
The director said that under no circumstances should interview notes leave the research team.
answer: The director said that under no circumstances should interview notes leave the research team.
explanation: The negative adjunct belongs inside the reported clause, where 'should' precedes its subject.

rationales.The director said that under no circumst: The fronted negative adjunct requires inversion within the embedded clause in this formal construction.
The negative adjunct belongs inside the reported clause, where 'should' precedes its subject.
rationales.Under no circumstances did the director: This denies that the director made a statement; it does not report a prohibition on sharing notes.
rationales.The director said that under no circumst: This reverses the prohibited action from leaving to remaining.

sentence: Which sentence preserves both time references?
setupText: The archive was incomplete when the study was conducted. Its missing material still weakens the conclusion today. Use formal conditional inversion to express the unreal alternative.
taskText: Which sentence preserves both time references?
text: The archive was incomplete when the study was conducted. Its missing material still weakens the conclusion today. Use formal conditional inversion to express the unreal alternative. Which sentence preserves both time references?
options: Were the conclusion stronger now, the archive would have been complete.
Had the archive been complete, the conclusion was stronger now.
Had the archive been complete, the conclusion would be stronger now.
Has the archive been complete, the conclusion would be stronger now.
answer: Had the archive been complete, the conclusion would be stronger now.
explanation: Inverted 'had ... been' sets an unreal past condition, while 'would be ... now' supplies its present consequence.

rationales.Were the conclusion stronger now, the ar: This reverses the explanatory direction, making the conclusion the condition for the archive's completeness.
rationales.Had the archive been complete, the concl: The asserted past 'was' does not express the unreal present result.
Inverted 'had ... been' sets an unreal past condition, while 'would be ... now' supplies its present consequence.
rationales.Has the archive been complete, the concl: 'Has' cannot replace past-perfect 'had' in this inverted counterfactual condition.

sentence: Which revision keeps the object contrast intact?
setupText: A committee accepts an idea as worth exploring but rejects the evidence currently offered for it. An editor prefers a compact formal contrast with 'not ... but'.
taskText: Which revision keeps the object contrast intact?
text: A committee accepts an idea as worth exploring but rejects the evidence currently offered for it. An editor prefers a compact formal contrast with 'not ... but'. Which revision keeps the object contrast intact?
options: The committee rejects not the idea but the evidence offered for it.
The committee rejects the idea, but not the evidence offered for it.
The committee rejects the idea as well as the evidence offered for it.
The committee does not reject either the idea or the evidence offered for it.
answer: The committee rejects not the idea but the evidence offered for it.
focusKey: coverage-inversion-and-emphasis-c1-1768:Delayed not in a formal object contrast
explanation: Delayed 'not' is legitimate in this formal paired contrast and restricts the correction to the verb's objects.

rationales.The committee rejects the idea, but not: This reverses which object is rejected.
rationales.The committee rejects the idea as well a: This adds rejection of the idea instead of excluding it from the rejection.
rationales.The committee does not reject either the: This denies the rejection of the evidence as well as the idea.
rationales.The committee rejects not the idea but t: Delayed 'not' is legitimate in this formal paired contrast and restricts the correction to the verb's objects.

sentence: Which pair completes both sentences with the intended meaning?
setupText: The key term is defined nowhere except the revised appendix. Compare two proposed openings: 'Only the revised appendix ...' and 'Only in the revised appendix ...'.
taskText: Which pair completes both sentences with the intended meaning?
text: The key term is defined nowhere except the revised appendix. Compare two proposed openings: 'Only the revised appendix ...' and 'Only in the revised appendix ...'. Which pair completes both sentences with the intended meaning?
options: does define the term / the author does define the term
does the term define / does the author define the term
defines the term / does the author define the term
defines the term / does the author defines the term
answer: defines the term / does the author define the term
explanation: The first only-phrase is the subject; the second is a fronted location adjunct, which triggers inversion.

rationales.defines the term / does the author defin: The first only-phrase is the subject; the second is a fronted location adjunct, which triggers inversion.
rationales.does define the term / the author does d: The first can use emphatic 'does', but the second lacks the inversion required by fronted 'Only in'.
rationales.does the term define / does the author d: The first reverses the grammatical roles and does not make the appendix the defining source.
rationales.defines the term / does the author defin: The second incorrectly puts an -s form after 'does'.

sentence: Which revision satisfies the requested construction?
setupText: The authors avoided broad claims because their sample was very small. Rewrite with 'Such' first, retaining that cause-result relationship.
taskText: Which revision satisfies the requested construction?
text: The authors avoided broad claims because their sample was very small. Rewrite with 'Such' first, retaining that cause-result relationship. Which revision satisfies the requested construction?
options: Such small was the sample that the authors avoided broad claims.
Such was the authors' caution that the small sample was not used to support broad claims.
Such was the sample's small size although the authors avoided broad claims.
Such was the small size of the sample that the authors avoided broad claims.
answer: Such was the small size of the sample that the authors avoided broad claims.
focusKey: coverage-inversion-and-emphasis-c1-1770:Such inversion with a noun-based degree expression
explanation: 'Such was + noun phrase' foregrounds degree; the that-clause gives the resulting restraint.

rationales.Such small was the sample that the autho: An adjective alone takes the pattern 'So small was ...'; 'such' here needs a noun phrase or the 'such was' construction.
rationales.Such was the small size of the sample th: 'Such was + noun phrase' foregrounds degree; the that-clause gives the resulting restraint.
rationales.Such was the authors' caution that the s: This makes the authors' degree of caution the cause instead of preserving the stated cause, the sample's small size.
rationales.Such was the sample's small size althoug: 'Although' substitutes concession for the requested degree-result relationship.

sentence: Which conclusion is warranted by this construction alone?
setupText: A project diary says, 'No sooner had the funding been approved than the timetable changed.'
taskText: Which conclusion is warranted by this construction alone?
text: A project diary says, 'No sooner had the funding been approved than the timetable changed.' Which conclusion is warranted by this construction alone?
options: The timetable changed before approval and caused it to be granted.
The timetable had to change as a condition of receiving approval.
The timetable changed almost immediately after approval.
The approval and timetable change are presented as exactly simultaneous.
answer: The timetable changed almost immediately after approval.
explanation: 'No sooner ... than' emphasizes near-immediate succession, but timing alone does not state causation.

rationales.The timetable changed before approval an: This reverses the temporal sequence and adds an unsupported cause.
rationales.The timetable had to change as a conditi: The construction presents two closely timed events, not a condition attached to approval.
rationales.The timetable changed almost immediately: 'No sooner ... than' emphasizes near-immediate succession, but timing alone does not state causation.
rationales.The approval and timetable change are pr: The construction orders one event just after another rather than asserting exact simultaneity.

sentence: What does B's parallel contrast do in this exchange?
setupText: A: 'But we do have the data.' B: 'The issue is not whether the data exist, but whether we can use them.'
taskText: What does B's parallel contrast do in this exchange?
text: A: 'But we do have the data.' B: 'The issue is not whether the data exist, but whether we can use them.' What does B's parallel contrast do in this exchange?
options: It concedes that the data do not exist.
Moves the discussion from possession of data to their usability.
It states that existing data must therefore be usable.
It replaces a question about usability with one about existence.
answer: Moves the discussion from possession of data to their usability.
explanation: The paired whether-clauses reject A's proposed issue as insufficient and identify the relevant question.

B sets existence aside rather than denying it.
rationales.It states that existing data must theref: B distinguishes existence from usability instead of treating the former as proof of the latter.
rationales.It replaces a question about usability w: This reverses the direction of B's shift.
rationales.Moves the discussion from possession of: The paired whether-clauses reject A's proposed issue as insufficient and identify the relevant question.

sentence: Which explanation correctly accounts for the different word orders?
setupText: Compare 'Little of the archive survived' and 'Little did the reviewers know about the missing files.'
taskText: Which explanation correctly accounts for the different word orders?
text: Compare 'Little of the archive survived' and 'Little did the reviewers know about the missing files.' Which explanation correctly accounts for the different word orders?
options: The first sentence is wrong because every fronted 'little' requires 'did'.
Little is part of the subject in 1 but a negative adverbial in 2.
The second sentence is a direct question because did precedes reviewers.
The difference is that survived is past but know is present.
answer: Little is part of the subject in 1 but a negative adverbial in 2.
explanation: A negative-quantity subject keeps ordinary order, whereas fronted negative 'little' as an adverbial calls for auxiliary inversion.

rationales.Little is part of the subject in 1 but a: A negative-quantity subject keeps ordinary order, whereas fronted negative 'little' as an adverbial calls for auxiliary inversion.
rationales.The first sentence is wrong because ever: 'Little of the archive' is a complete subject and does not require inversion.
rationales.The second sentence is a direct question: Fronted negative expressions can produce inversion in declarative statements as well as questions.
rationales.The difference is that survived is past: The second sentence is also past; 'did' carries its tense.

sentence: What does this wording deny?
setupText: An analyst writes, 'It was not because the baseline shifted that the comparison failed; the two groups had been measured differently.'
taskText: What does this wording deny?
text: An analyst writes, 'It was not because the baseline shifted that the comparison failed; the two groups had been measured differently.' What does this wording deny?
options: That the baseline shifted at all.
That the comparison failed.
That the groups were measured differently.
That a shifted baseline caused the comparison's failure.
answer: That a shifted baseline caused the comparison's failure.
explanation: Negation targets the because-clause as an explanation, while the following clause offers a different cause.

The cleft negates the proposed reason; it does not settle whether the baseline changed.
rationales.That a shifted baseline caused the compa: Negation targets the because-clause as an explanation, while the following clause offers a different cause.
The failure is treated as the event requiring explanation, not denied.
rationales.That the groups were measured differentl: The final clause asserts that difference as the alternative explanation.

sentence: Which pair preserves both meanings and uses formal standard order?
setupText: Use 'Not a single applicant' first in two sentences: one says nobody received an explanation; the other says the manager consulted nobody.
taskText: Which pair preserves both meanings and uses formal standard order?
text: Use 'Not a single applicant' first in two sentences: one says nobody received an explanation; the other says the manager consulted nobody. Which pair preserves both meanings and uses formal standard order?
options: Not a single applicant received an explanation. / Not a single applicant did the manager consult.
Not a single applicant did receive an explanation. / Not a single applicant the manager consulted.
Not a single applicant received an explanation. / Not a single applicant consulted the manager.
Not a single applicant received an explanation. / Not a single applicant did consult the manager.
answer: Not a single applicant received an explanation. / Not a single applicant did the manager consult.
explanation: The negative subject in the first stays before its verb; the fronted negative object in the second triggers 'did the manager consult'.

rationales.Not a single applicant did receive an ex: The first can be emphatic, but the second fronted negative object requires inversion in the requested formal style.
rationales.Not a single applicant received an expla: The second makes applicants the consulting agents rather than the people whom the manager did not consult.
The negative subject in the first stays before its verb; the fronted negative object in the second triggers 'did the manager consult'.
The second again makes the applicant the subject; emphatic 'did' does not preserve the manager's role.

sentence: Which formal rewrite preserves that logical restriction?
setupText: The estimate cannot be trusted unless its limitation is disclosed. Rewrite with 'Only if' first, preserving the requirement without promising that disclosure alone makes the estimate trustworthy.
taskText: Which formal rewrite preserves that logical restriction?
text: The estimate cannot be trusted unless its limitation is disclosed. Rewrite with 'Only if' first, preserving the requirement without promising that disclosure alone makes the estimate trustworthy. Which formal rewrite preserves that logical restriction?
options: Only if the estimate can be trusted is the limitation disclosed.
Only if the limitation is disclosed can the estimate be trusted.
If the limitation is disclosed, the estimate can be trusted.
Only if the limitation is not disclosed can the estimate be trusted.
answer: Only if the limitation is disclosed can the estimate be trusted.
explanation: The fronted condition remains necessary for trust; the main clause inverts 'can' without making disclosure sufficient.

rationales.Only if the limitation is disclosed can: The fronted condition remains necessary for trust; the main clause inverts 'can' without making disclosure sufficient.
rationales.Only if the estimate can be trusted is t: This makes trust a requirement for disclosure, reversing the implication.
rationales.If the limitation is disclosed, the esti: This presents disclosure as sufficient, whereas the original only made it necessary.
rationales.Only if the limitation is not disclosed: This makes non-disclosure the condition, contradicting the original restriction.

sentence: Which revision follows that focus instruction without adding a new claim?
setupText: An editor wants to put the rejected priority first while preserving 'The report emphasizes accuracy rather than speed.'
taskText: Which revision follows that focus instruction without adding a new claim?
text: An editor wants to put the rejected priority first while preserving 'The report emphasizes accuracy rather than speed.' Which revision follows that focus instruction without adding a new claim?
options: Rather than speed, the report emphasizes accuracy.
Rather than accuracy, the report emphasizes speed.
Only when speed increases does the report emphasize accuracy.
Not only speed but also accuracy is emphasized in the report.
answer: Rather than speed, the report emphasizes accuracy.
explanation: The contrasting phrase can be fronted without auxiliary inversion; it places the rejected priority first.

rationales.Rather than accuracy, the report emphasi: This reverses which priority is accepted and which is rejected.
rationales.Rather than speed, the report emphasizes: The contrasting phrase can be fronted without auxiliary inversion; it places the rejected priority first.
rationales.Only when speed increases does the repor: This introduces a time condition absent from the source.
rationales.Not only speed but also accuracy is emph: This changes a preference contrast into additive emphasis on both priorities.

sentence: Which revision accurately carries out the proposal?
setupText: The hearing had barely begun when the recording failed. An editor proposes using 'Scarcely' first while retaining the original sequence and passive-free wording.
taskText: Which revision accurately carries out the proposal?
text: The hearing had barely begun when the recording failed. An editor proposes using 'Scarcely' first while retaining the original sequence and passive-free wording. Which revision accurately carries out the proposal?
options: Scarcely had the hearing begun when the recording failed.
Scarcely had the recording failed when the hearing began.
Scarcely had the hearing been begun when the recording failed.
Scarcely the hearing had begun when the recording failed.
answer: Scarcely had the hearing begun when the recording failed.
focusKey: coverage-inversion-and-emphasis-c1-1778:Scarcely fronting preserves aspect and event order
explanation: 'Scarcely had' preserves the earlier, barely begun event; 'when' introduces the interruption.

rationales.Scarcely had the recording failed when t: This swaps the closely sequenced events.
rationales.Scarcely had the hearing been begun when: This introduces a passive reading and an implied agent, which the instruction excludes.
rationales.Scarcely the hearing had begun when the: The fronted negative adverb requires auxiliary-before-subject order in this formal pattern.
rationales.Scarcely had the hearing begun when the: 'Scarcely had' preserves the earlier, barely begun event; 'when' introduces the interruption.

sentence: Which editorial judgment is accurate?
setupText: Compare 'What the witness did was repeat the warning' and 'What the witness did was to repeat the warning.'
taskText: Which editorial judgment is accurate?
text: Compare 'What the witness did was repeat the warning' and 'What the witness did was to repeat the warning.' Which editorial judgment is accurate?
options: Only the first is grammatical because did forbids to anywhere later.
Both are grammatical, with no change in the reported action.
Only the second is grammatical because every complement of was needs to.
Both are grammatical, but only the second says the warning was actually repeated.
answer: Both are grammatical, with no change in the reported action.
explanation: The do-pseudo-cleft permits both a bare infinitive and a to-infinitive without changing who repeated the warning.

rationales.Only the first is grammatical because di: The 'to' is in the focused complement after 'was', not directly after auxiliary 'did'.
rationales.Only the second is grammatical because e: A bare infinitive is also allowed in this do-pseudo-cleft, and many other complements of be are not infinitives.
rationales.Both are grammatical, with no change in: The do-pseudo-cleft permits both a bare infinitive and a to-infinitive without changing who repeated the warning.
rationales.Both are grammatical, but only the secon: Both identify repeating the warning as what the witness did; the extra 'to' does not change actuality.

sentence: Which conclusion is justified by that sentence alone?
setupText: A reviewer writes, 'Nowhere in the published policy does it say that late appeals are automatic.'
taskText: Which conclusion is justified by that sentence alone?
text: A reviewer writes, 'Nowhere in the published policy does it say that late appeals are automatic.' Which conclusion is justified by that sentence alone?
options: Late appeals are expressly prohibited by the published policy.
Late appeals cannot be approved by any route.
The policy promises that each late appeal will be considered individually.
The published policy contains no statement granting automatic late appeals.
answer: The published policy contains no statement granting automatic late appeals.
explanation: 'Nowhere in' restricts the negative claim to what this document says.

rationales.Late appeals are expressly prohibited by: Absence of an automatic-appeal statement is not an express prohibition on appeals.
rationales.The published policy contains no stateme: 'Nowhere in' restricts the negative claim to what this document says.
rationales.Late appeals cannot be approved by any r: The sentence makes no claim about every possible approval route.
rationales.The policy promises that each late appea: An individual-review promise cannot be inferred from the absence of an automatic-appeal provision.
